headline: With every lane forced onto a plain inline style, next-yak's CSS-variable indirection is exposed as a real cost: it roughly doubles the styled API's per-instance time, and buys a value that stays inside CSS.

microbench.why: `next-yak-9.7` renders at 0.642 ms/1k here against 1.23 in the Example `dyn-fair`, where the same value rides a custom property. The profile names the difference: with the value in a plain inline style the fold rewrites the styled component to a `<div className>` and the library slice is 0.256 ms; with the value in a `--var` the interpolation forces a `Yak` runtime component back onto every element and the slice reaches 0.704 ms. `vanilla` at 0.603 ms/1k is the floor and the folded lane is 6% off it.

autocannon.why: `vanilla` 1,190 req/s and `next-yak-9.7` 1,180, a tie inside the measurement. The 9.6.0 runtime at 624 req/s is what one React component per styled element costs on the same source, and `foldStatic: false` at 892 shows how much of the gap folding alone closes.

attribution.why: `vanilla` costs 0.760 ms, react-dom plus a style attribute. `next-yak-9.7` costs 1.06 ms with a 0.256 ms library slice, and the profile shows no runtime package at all: the fold has replaced the component with a plain element, and what is left is 17.8 ms of react-dom against `vanilla`'s 13.0, the cost of the emitted attributes. Turning folding off puts 3.79 ms of runtime back into the profile.

hydrate.why: 50.8 ms for `next-yak-9.7` and 51.6 for `vanilla`, both pure JS with no style or layout in the span, since neither has anything to inject. Folding is worth 3.3 ms of the difference to the `foldStatic: false` build.

inp.why: One inline style is rewritten and every lane lands at 7.1-7.6 ms, a single measurement wide. Nothing in this case can distinguish them on an interaction.

mount.why: `vanilla` 68.1 ms and `next-yak-9.7` 68.3, one sheet parse and one paint. The 9.6.0 runtime reaches 75.7 ms because it renders a component per element before that paint.

renderTiming.why: One recalculation, one layout, one paint everywhere, counts identical. Recalc cost sits at 0.116-0.256 ms, which is noise on a case where the browser only has to read a style attribute.

payload.why: `vanilla` ships 5.50 kB and `next-yak-9.7` 6.53, the whole difference being the 1.10 kB of next-yak runtime that survives the fold. The inline-style spelling costs 190 B more markup than the custom-property spelling in `dyn-fair`, since `transform:translateX(37px)` is longer than a variable assignment.

nsweep.why: `vanilla` 2.68 ms and `next-yak-9.7` 2.82 at n=4,000, both linear. The same lane costs 5.32 ms in `dyn-fair`, so the variable indirection is close to a factor of two once it is multiplied by n, and `foldStatic: false` at 3.87 ms is where the fold stops covering for it.

crossCase: This case exists to price one thing against the Example `dyn-fair` shown above: next-yak's CSS-variable path costs `next-yak-9.7` 0.642 to 1.23 ms/1k and 2.82 to 5.32 ms at n=4,000, because an interpolation the fold cannot resolve keeps a `Yak` runtime component on every element (library slice 0.256 to 0.704 ms). What that buys is that the value lives in CSS, so it can be read inside media queries, pseudo-states and nested rules, and that the naive spelling in the Example `dyn-translate` shown above costs exactly the same as the tuned one. Every other library reaches the inline-style shape only by hand, and pays the `dyn-translate` figures until someone does.
